rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shuʿara presents an argumentative inquiry whose ending repudiates idols; al-Saffat stages a sharper challenge ending in idol-breaking and the fire, so the stronger wording suits its confrontation.
rows.anchor: فثمة فرق كبير بين النهايتين وبين السياقين

rows.speaker: درة التنزيل
rows.claim: The source explains bare ما as “what thing”; ماذا can be parsed as ما plus relative ذا, or as one interrogative meaning “what thing,” and is more emphatic in either parse.
rows.anchor: جاء في (درة التنزيل) في هاتين الآيتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Shuʿara the question serves as a prompt: the idolaters answer that they worship idols, then cite their forefathers when Abraham asks whether the idols hear, help, or harm.
rows.anchor: فلما قصد في الأول التنبيه كانت (ما) كافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In al-Saffat ماذا is a rebuke, followed by further taunting rather than a request for their answer; this matches the story's forceful confrontation.
rows.anchor: وأما (ماذا تعبدون) ؟ في سورة الصافات فإنها تقريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extended pronunciation of السبيل in the damned people's lament suits their raised, prolonged crying; the unextended form in 33:4 occurs outside that lamenting scene.
rows.anchor: فمد (السبيل) في حين قال في الآية الرابعة من السورة نفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding أن after لما in al-Ankabut suits the fuller account and suggests prolonged waiting and anticipation before the angels arrive, unlike the briefer Hud account.
rows.anchor: ولذا حسن ذكر (أن) في العنكبوت دون هود مراعاة للتبسط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ankabut details the people's offenses, including coming to men, cutting the road, and public indecency; Hud compresses their behavior as doing evil deeds, suiting the longer account.
rows.anchor: ففصل في عمل السيئات ما لم يفصله في هود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot's distress and expectation of rescue are more explicit in al-Ankabut; deliverance is promised there to Abraham and Lot, with no comparable wording in Hud.
rows.anchor: ومنها التصريح بلفظ التنجية ومجيء الفرج في سورة العنكبوت مرتين

words: قَالَ رَبِّ انصُرْنِي عَلَى الْقَوْمِ الْمُفْسِدِينَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After his people deny him and demand punishment, Lot prays for help against them; the author contrasts this with Hud, where no such prayer is narrated.
rows.anchor: ومنها دعاؤه ربه أن ينصره على قومه بعدما كذبوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added أن in Jacob's reunion scene separates لما from the arrival and evokes his intense longing and the way each moment of waiting seemed prolonged.
rows.anchor: فزاد (أن) بعد (لم) وذلك لمناسبة حالة الانتظار والترقب

rows.speaker: معترك الأقران
rows.claim: The cited work says أن suits the herald's arrival after a long period and expresses the temporal delay.
rows.anchor: جاء في (معترك الأقران) : "فإن قلت:

rows.speaker: مصطفى صادق الرافعي
rows.claim: Al-Rafiʿi reads أن as picturing the interval and distance before the herald reached Jacob, whose anxious anticipation makes the arrival especially vivid.
rows.anchor: وذكر مصطفى صادق الرافعي أن المراد بذلك:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added أن and separation after لما portray Moses as pausing before his second attempt to strike; the first incident instead uses successive fa clauses for immediate action.
rows.anchor: فزاد (أن) للدلالة على ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses first rebukes his companion as plainly misguided; the companion then fears Moses means to strike him, supporting the author's reading that Moses was not rushing into action.
rows.anchor: ومما يدلك على تمهله وعدم اندفاعه في المرة الثانية تعنيفه لصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author states a general principle: wording may be added in one place and omitted in another according to meaning and context, as the examples that follow illustrate.
rows.anchor: كلمة أو أكثر في موضع، ولا يذكرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An-Nisa adds مقتا because marrying one's father's wife is an act whose perpetrator is loathed and regarded as repulsive by sound natures; in other respects it is likened to fornication.
rows.anchor: متزوج امرأة أبيه فاعل رذيلة يمقت فاعلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author adduces another wording contrast: al-Taghabun adds expiation of sins before the promise of gardens, while al-Talaq mentions entry into gardens without that phrase.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قوله تعالى: {وَمَن يُؤْمِن بالله وَيَعْمَلْ صَالِحاً يُكَفِّرْ عَنْهُ سَيِّئَاتِهِ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraf embeds Moses and Pharaoh in a wider history of the Children of Israel, while al-Shuʿara recounts their story in detail through Pharaoh's drowning; the latter is one part of the former's broader account.
rows.anchor: إن موضوع القصة في سورة الأعراف هو تاريخ من بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The al-Shuʿara narrative is built around detailed event-by-event telling and strong confrontation; al-Aʿraf is concise and lacks the same force of challenge.
rows.anchor: إن القصة في سورة الشعراء تتسم بسمتين بارزتين هما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraf opens with Moses' short message to Pharaoh; al-Shuʿara begins earlier, with God's commission, Moses' fears and request for Aaron, and God's reassurance.
rows.anchor: أما في الشعراء فقد بدأت بالأحداث السابقة لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shuʿara expands Pharaoh's accusation that he raised Moses and that Moses killed an Egyptian; Moses acknowledges the deed and explains that he fled from them in fear.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر فرعون منته عليه بتربيته في بيته وأنه فعل ما فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers Pharaoh's reminder of his upbringing by citing God's gift of judgment and messengership, then overturns Pharaoh's claimed favor by pointing to his enslavement of the Israelites.
rows.anchor: فأقر بذلك موسى وذكر من أمر فراره منهم ما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Moses answers Pharaoh's question about the Lord of the worlds, Pharaoh offers no counterargument and instead tries to turn his audience against Moses.
rows.anchor: فلا يرد عليه فرعون بالحجة ولكن حاول أن يؤلب عليه من حوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' reply that God is Lord of East and West, followed by “if you reason,” pointedly answers Pharaoh's accusation of madness by challenging their rationality.
rows.anchor: ما رماه به من الجنون وعدم العقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once argument fails, Pharaoh threatens Moses with prison; this exchange is absent from al-Aʿraf because that telling is shorter and less confrontational.
rows.anchor: ولما أعيتْه الحيلة وأعوزه المنطق توعده وتهدده بالسجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraf has Pharaoh's nobles speak, consistent with his royal hauteur; in al-Shuʿara Pharaoh speaks to his council himself because the debate has unsettled him and exposed his inability to answer.
rows.anchor: في حين أن الذي قال في آية الشعراء هو فرعون نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Shuʿara adds “with his magic” to suit its detailed narrative and intensify Pharaoh's allegation that Moses is a magician.
rows.anchor: وزاد كلمة (بسحره) لمناسبة مقام التفصيل في الشعراء
